strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: adapting prior-data fitted/tabular foundation models to heterogeneous graph node prediction, where feature and label spaces vary across datasets.

The proposed architecture is conceptually clean: starting from LimiX and inserting sparse attention-based message-passing adapters into each block is a plausible way to add graph inductive bias while preserving the tabular PFN interface.

The synthetic graph prior is interesting and reasonably motivated, combining degree-corrected SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCMs to generate attributed graphs with community/core-periphery structure.

The empirical results are promising in the finetuning regime: GraphPFN is best on many of the evaluated datasets where it fits in memory, with especially large gains on artnet-exp, hm-prices, artnet-views, facebook, amazon-ratings, and questions.
The paper includes strong baseline families, including tuned classic GNNs, LightGBM with neighborhood feature aggregation, and recent G2T-FM variants with TabPFNv2/LimiX backbones.
The limitations section is unusually candid about scalability, prior mismatch, limited ablations, class-count limits, and restriction to node-level tasks.
weaknesses: The central contribution is difficult to reproduce from the manuscript. The graph prior is the core of the method, but the actual hyperparameter distributions for SBM composition, preferential attachment, graph sizes, densities, SCM architectures, LapPE usage, and target/feature sampling are not specified in enough detail to recreate the pretraining data.

Experimental details are too thin for a main-track foundation-model paper. The appendix does not provide downstream hyperparameter search spaces, finetuning schedules, batch/memory settings, preprocessing details beyond limited PCA notes, or code/model release information, despite the claim of a publicly available implementation.

The evidence for the proposed prior and pretraining objective is limited. There is only one ablation comparing pretrained versus random graph adapters; there are no ablations of the graph prior components, graph-aware SCM, masked graph modeling loss, adapter placement/depth, freezing strategy, or initialization from LimiX versus training more components.

The in-context learning results are mixed and weaker than the narrative suggests. GraphPFN ICL is substantially worse than G2T-LimiX on hm-prices, city-roads-M, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, questions, and wiki-cs, and sometimes worse than classic GNNs. This undercuts the foundation-model/ICL claim, leaving the strongest evidence mainly in supervised finetuning.

Scalability is a major unresolved issue. GraphPFN OOMs on several larger datasets, including city-reviews, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, and pubmed in finetuning, while the paper claims strong results on datasets up to roughly 50k nodes and frames the method as a graph foundation model. The current whole-graph processing requirement sharply limits practical reach.

The state-of-the-art claim is too broad. Results are reported only on a selected subset of node-level datasets with at most 10 classes and mostly small/medium graphs, with several OOM omissions and no evaluation on link prediction, graph-level prediction, larger-class tasks, or larger graphs.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially that GraphPFN does not rely on hand-crafted features and that poor performance is mainly a non-fundamental prior-mismatch issue. Those hypotheses are plausible but not experimentally validated.

Ethics and broader impact are not discussed. While the work appears low risk, graph foundation models can be applied to social, behavioral, and recommendation networks, so privacy, bias, and misuse considerations should at least be acknowledged.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: making prior-data fitted networks useful for graph node prediction rather than relying only on hand-crafted graph features passed into tabular foundation models.

The high-level architecture is sensible: starting from LimiX and inserting adjacency-masked attention/message-passing adapters is a plausible way to preserve heterogeneous-feature handling while adding graph inductive bias.
The experimental tables include reasonably strong baselines, including improved classic GNNs, LightGBM with neighborhood feature aggregation, and G2T-FM variants with TabPFNv2 and LimiX backbones.

The authors are fairly candid about several limitations, including poor scalability, limited ablations, lack of support for more than 10 classes, and gaps in the proposed graph prior for domains such as traffic networks.

Finetuned GraphPFN does show strong results on the subset of datasets where it runs, including clear gains over G2T-LimiX on several GraphLand datasets such as artnet-exp, hm-prices, and artnet-views.
weaknesses: The central contribution, the synthetic graph prior, is not specified with enough detail to be reproducible or scientifically assessable. The paper says many hyperparameters are sampled from distributions, but the actual distributions, ranges, and generation algorithm details are largely absent.

The evidence does not support the broad claims about a successful graph foundation model. In-context performance is mixed and often worse than G2T-LimiX, e.g. hm-prices, city-roads-M, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, questions, and wiki-cs. The strongest claims rely mainly on finetuning, where GraphPFN cannot run on several larger datasets due to OOM.

Scalability is a serious technical weakness rather than a minor limitation. The method processes the whole dataset at once and fails to finetune on city-reviews, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, and pubmed, undermining claims about practical graph foundation modeling.

Ablations are far too limited for a paper whose novelty is a combination of architecture, graph prior, LimiX initialization, masked graph modeling, LapPE, and finetuning protocol. The only substantial ablation compares pretrained versus random graph adapters; there is no convincing isolation of the proposed prior, MGM objective, adapter placement, graph generator components, or LimiX dependence.

The experimental protocol is under-described. Hyperparameter tuning details for GNNs, finetuning budgets, optimizer settings for downstream tasks, batch/memory settings, and exact preprocessing are not sufficiently reported. PCA is applied to some datasets in the appendix, but the broader preprocessing and fairness implications are not carefully analyzed.

The state-of-the-art framing is overstated. Results are reported on a limited set of node-level datasets, with exclusions for larger tasks and more than 10 classes, and without comparisons to several broader graph foundation model families beyond G2T-FM-style approaches.

The paper evaluates on GraphLand datasets during pretraining every 100 steps and then reports GraphLand as a main benchmark. Although the authors state this was post-hoc and not used for selection, this creates avoidable concerns about benchmark exposure and researcher degrees of freedom.

Presentation is readable but often too high-level where precision is needed. Key architectural and training details, especially around sparse attention adapters, target embeddings for MGM, downstream finetuning, and the graph prior, are described narratively rather than in a way that would let others implement the method reliably.

Reproducibility is weak: there is no clear code or model release statement, and the method requires substantial compute: 500k steps on 8 A100 80GB GPUs for about 6 days. Combined with missing prior distributions and limited implementation details, independent verification would be difficult.

The paper does not meaningfully discuss research ethics, environmental cost, or possible misuse. The ethical risk may be modest, but the compute cost and deployment implications of graph models on social/behavioral datasets deserve at least brief treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: extending PFN/tabular foundation model ideas to heterogeneous graph node-level tasks without relying only on hand-crafted graph features.

The proposed architecture is sensible and technically well motivated: starting from LimiX and inserting sparse graph-neighborhood attention adapters preserves the tabular PFN machinery while adding learnable graph message passing.

The synthetic graph prior is a meaningful contribution in itself, combining multi-level degree-corrected SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCM attribute generation to create diverse attributed graph tasks.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad, covering GraphLand plus classic datasets, classification and regression, homophily and heterophily, and comparisons to strong tuned GNNs, LightGBM-NFA, and G2T-FM variants.
Finetuned GraphPFN obtains strong results, often improving over G2T-LimiX and tuned GNN baselines; the random-adapter ablation supports the claim that graph-prior pretraining matters.
The paper is clearly written, and the limitations section is candid about scalability, prior mismatch, limited ablations, task scope, and inherited LimiX constraints.
weaknesses: The strongest results are mostly in the finetuning setting, while the in-context/foundation-model claim is less uniformly supported: GraphPFN ICL is substantially worse than G2T-LimiX on several datasets such as hm-prices, city-roads-M, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, questions, and wiki-cs.

Scalability is a material limitation. The model requires whole-graph processing, OOMs on multiple larger datasets in finetuning, and therefore does not yet convincingly support broad graph foundation model use beyond small/medium transductive settings.

The evaluation leaves some ambiguity about fairness and cost. GraphPFN is pretrained for 500k steps on 8 A100s and then finetuned, but the compute/parameter/tuning budgets relative to GNN and G2T-FM baselines are not fully analyzed.

Ablations are limited. The paper does not isolate key prior components, the MGM objective, adapter placement/depth, freezing choices, or the effect of different graph-generating distributions, making it hard to know which design choices are essential.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript: many prior hyperparameter distributions, finetuning details, baseline search spaces, and code/model-release information are either absent or deferred too lightly, despite the method depending heavily on a complex synthetic generator and expensive pretraining.

The use of bidirectional graph adapters over labeled and unlabeled nodes should be discussed more carefully in relation to the PFN masking protocol and transductive assumptions, since query nodes can exchange feature/structure information through the graph even when labels are masked.

The significance is promising but not yet decisive: the work is a useful step toward graph PFNs, but the current method is limited to node-level tasks, at most 10 classes natively, and datasets whose topology/features match the proposed prior.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and technically plausible extension of PFNs to node-level graph learning: LimiX is augmented with sparse attention-based graph adapters and pretrained on synthetic attributed graphs. The architecture is well motivated and preserves the variable-feature handling of the tabular backbone while adding graph-local information flow.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the targeted setting, covering 13 datasets across GraphLand and classic graph benchmarks, classification and regression, homophilic and heterophilic graphs, and comparisons to strong GNNs, prior graph foundation models, G2T-FM, and TAG. The finetuned GraphPFN results are consistently strong, with best average ranks and wins on most datasets.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses: pretraining curves, comparisons to simpler graph priors, a comparison against randomly initialized graph adapters, and statistics comparing the synthetic prior to real graph properties. These support the claim that both graph-aware pretraining and the proposed prior matter.

Presentation is generally strong. The motivation, architecture, prior construction, and experimental protocol are easy to follow, and the limitations section is honest about scalability, domain coverage of the prior, class-count limits, and lack of support for graph-level/link-prediction tasks.

The contribution is significant because it demonstrates that PFN-style synthetic pretraining can be effective for graph node tasks, rather than only tabular tasks or graph-tabularization pipelines. This is a useful step for graph foundation models.
weaknesses: The central foundation-model claim is somewhat narrower than the framing suggests. The method is limited to node-level prediction, small/medium full-graph inference, at most 10 classes, and datasets whose graph structures resemble the synthetic prior; these constraints reduce generality.

The ICL results are strong but not uniformly dominant. GraphPFN underperforms G2T-LimiX or TAG on several datasets in the ICL setting, and the strongest claims mainly rely on finetuning plus ensembling, where the distinction from a strong pretrained initialization with graph adapters is less clean.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the provided PDF, and important details such as exact prior hyperparameter distributions, finetuning hyperparameters, tuning budgets for baselines, and model/checkpoint availability are not fully specified in the main text.

The use of benchmark test-set evaluations throughout pretraining is described as post-hoc and not used for selection, but it is still a concerning practice because it creates potential benchmark awareness and makes it harder to rule out informal overfitting or reporting bias.

The comparison to baselines may involve unequal compute and tuning conditions. GraphPFN benefits from substantial pretraining, full finetuning, and 10-member ensembling, while the paper gives limited detail on whether all competing models received comparable tuning and inference budgets.

The graph prior is interesting but partly heuristic. The paper shows coverage of some graph statistics, but the synthetic-vs-real match is incomplete for cases such as road networks and long average path lengths, and the analysis does not fully establish why the chosen prior should generalize beyond the evaluated domains.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: adapting prior-data fitted/tabular foundation models to graph node-level tasks, where feature heterogeneity and limited cross-domain graph data are genuine obstacles.

GraphPFN is a plausible and useful architectural extension of LimiX: sparse neighbor attention adapters are a natural way to add graph message passing while preserving the PFN-style in-context interface.

The empirical tables cover both classification and regression, GraphLand and classic datasets, and include several relevant baselines, including strong tabular/PFN-based graph methods such as G2T-LimiX and TAG.
The limitations section is unusually candid about scalability, domain coverage of the synthetic prior, class-count constraints, and restriction to node-level tasks.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. In-context performance is mixed: GraphPFN often improves over GNNs, but is not consistently better than G2T-LimiX, and loses on several datasets such as tolokers-2, avazu-ctr, and city-roads-M in Table 1. The most impressive results rely on full finetuning plus ensembling, which is less distinctive as a foundation-model contribution.

The novelty is incremental. The method is largely LimiX plus sparse graph-attention adapters, pretrained on a synthetic graph prior. This is a reasonable idea, but the manuscript does not establish a deep new mechanism or theory beyond combining known PFN, GNN attention, SBM/PA priors, and masked graph modeling ingredients.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank, and key implementation details are underspecified, especially the exact graph-prior hyperparameter distributions, LimiX checkpoint/configuration, adapter dimensions, tuning budgets, finetuning schedules, and baseline search spaces.

The synthetic prior is not convincingly validated. The prior is motivated visually and through a few aggregate graph statistics, but several real datasets fall outside the synthetic ranges or assumptions, e.g. road-network distances and domain-specific structures. The ablation against simpler random graph models is only first-stage pretraining, so it does not isolate the contribution of the full prior.

The evaluation risks overclaiming. The paper monitors test-set performance during pretraining for learning curves, asserts this was post-hoc, but the protocol still raises concerns about hidden iteration on the benchmark. There is also no strong discussion of dataset overlap, benchmark reuse, or possible contamination from pretrained LimiX/related models.

The comparison with task-specific GNNs is incomplete for a state-of-the-art claim. The paper reports tuned classic GNNs, but does not provide enough budget details to judge fairness against a large pretrained model with ensembling and full-graph transductive access. Compute, memory, and latency comparisons are also missing despite scalability being a major practical issue.

Important ablations are missing or too narrow: there is no clean decomposition of gains from LimiX initialization, graph adapters, masked graph modeling, random features, ensembling, and finetuning; the random-adapter ablation only addresses one part of the story.

Presentation is generally readable, but the paper sometimes makes broad claims about graph foundation models and generalizability from a relatively small set of medium-scale node-prediction datasets, with no link prediction, graph-level tasks, very large graphs, or domains beyond the chosen benchmarks.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and technically coherent extension of PFNs to graph node-level tasks: synthetic graph-prior pretraining, LimiX initialization, and sparse attention-based graph adapters are well-motivated and fit the PFN framework.

The empirical results are strong. GraphPFN is evaluated on diverse GraphLand and classic graph datasets, covers classification and regression, and compares against tuned GNNs, earlier GFMs, G2T-FM, and TAG. Finetuned GraphPFN, especially with ensembling, achieves the best average ranks and wins on most datasets.

The ablations support the main story: simpler random graph priors underperform the proposed prior in most cases, and replacing pretrained graph adapters with random adapters substantially degrades finetuned performance, suggesting that the graph-specific pretraining is not merely cosmetic.
The manuscript is clear and well organized. The graph prior, architecture, pretraining objective, evaluation settings, and limitations are described in enough detail to understand the contribution.
The limitations discussion is honest and useful, explicitly noting scaling problems, domain bias of the graph prior, the dependence on LimiX class-count limits, and restriction to node-level tasks.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not fully satisfactory. The abstract says code is available but the URL appears missing, and many details needed to exactly reproduce the graph prior and hyperparameter distributions are only described at a high level. Given the large 8xA100 pretraining cost, released code/checkpoints and precise prior specifications are important.

The evaluation, while broad, is still concentrated on small- and medium-scale node prediction datasets with at most 10 classes. This matches current TFM constraints but limits the strength of the broader “graph foundation model” claim.

The paper evaluates intermediate checkpoints on GraphLand test sets during pretraining and says this was only post-hoc. This is plausible, but it is still an avoidable source of concern; validation-only monitoring or held-out pretraining diagnostics would be cleaner.

The gains over G2T-LimiX are not uniform in pure ICL: GraphPFN loses on some regression datasets such as avazu-ctr and city-roads-M before ensembling/finetuning. The paper could more sharply distinguish where the graph prior helps versus where the tabular backbone already carries most performance.

Compute and inference costs are under-discussed. GraphPFN processes the whole graph jointly, uses ensembling in several headline results, and adds graph attention adapters, but the paper does not provide runtime/memory comparisons against G2T-FM, TAG, or tuned GNNs.

Some architectural and objective choices are not fully ablated, including the number/location of graph adapters, the masked graph modeling loss coefficient, LapPE use in the synthetic SCM, and random feature augmentation at evaluation time. This leaves some uncertainty about which components are essential.
